title: Why your L.O.I. looks Stupid
content: Kind: captions Language: en Welcome to Dealmakers. I'm Sarah Sharp. I'm a real deal attorney who helps people buy and sell businesses every day. And I'm going to tell you one of the things that's probably in your letter of intent makes you look like an idiot and makes your sellers think that you're not qualified to run their business. So you in this scenario have a letter of intent and maybe you've sent a lot of them out and you haven't gotten a lot of feedback or you've gotten just kind of a rope decline, decline, decline. Now you're wondering what you might be doing wrong and it could be nothing cuz that just happens sometimes. There is one mistake that I see that's being perpetuated all over this YouTube platform and LinkedIn and I want to get in front of it right now. Before I jump in though, if you do find this content valuable, please like and subscribe or share it with your friends and neighbors and check out dealacademy.org for some courses on how you can become the expert on the deal process and not have to rely on other folks to do all that for you. So, what are you missing? What are you doing wrong? There is a mythical unicorn term out there that is 0% interest on a seller financed deal. I don't know who started thinking that that was a thing that really happens, but I've seen a lot of folks come across my desk thinking that that is an attractive offer, which is neither here nor there. But even if a 100% seller finance deal is just not a thing that happens at any interest rate, if you are making an offer and a portion of that offer is either going to come from the bank or it's going to be cash that the seller receives at closing in any other way and then a portion of that offer is going to be a note, a loan document where the seller is basically loaning you money to be paid back later. That's called a seller note. If you're going to have portion of your deal, it's a seller note or seller finance, you need an interest rate for that loan document. And for some reason, a lot of folks think that 0% interest loans are a thing and they make you look really silly if you don't know that they're not a good idea. So why aren't they a good idea? Why doesn't the seller like them? I mean, it's not just a financial thing. So yes, the seller wants more money and interest rate secures that for them. Another reason relatedly is the seller wants to think that if you get a chance, you might pay them back. And if you have a 0% loan, it would never make financial sense for you to pay that back. You should ride that out and make the minimum payments until the very last payment date. So, that's not attractive from a deal structure perspective, but that's not really the thing that makes you look dumb. I mean, that's just a less attractive deal term. Every deal offering has those. Well, what makes you look silly is that you haven't identified that that brings a lot of risk into play for the seller because they might be subject to or they will be subject to imputed interest income, which is a concept that the IRS uses to say anybody who gets a below market loan has to pay taxes as though they made interest at a market rate. So, what does that mean? Unless you're subject to one of very narrow exceptions. If you have a loan principle of $100,000 and the applicable federal rate, Google it. You have short-term, midterm, long-term loans that you can cross reference and figure out what the feds think the fair market rate is. Let's say that that's 4%. So, if the applicable rate is 4% and you had a 2% loan on $100,000, then you were supposed to make $4,000 on that and interest, but you made two. So, you're going to be paying taxes as though you made four. So, if you have a $10,000 loan principal, AFR is 3%, the interest actually paid is 200, you're going to pay 100. Your taxes as though you paid you got paid an additional 100. So, there's a tax liability. Obviously, when you have a 0% loan, there's a quite big difference between 0%, especially if there's a pretty hefty loan principle. There's quite a big difference between 0% on several hundred,000 and 4.5% on several hundred,000. So, that's real tax liability that's borne by the seller. That's one of the reasons that people don't really like it when there's a 0% interest loan. Obviously, we also have cost of living increases and everything like that. So, with inflation, you really it's almost a reverse interest rate if you're at 0%. But that is why a smart offer will at least address that by saying AFR, applicable federal rate is the bare minimum interest that they'll pay on that seller note. If you do offer a 0% loan, you're asking the seller to take on that tax liability in addition to loaning you money at a cost to them essentially, in addition to the risks associated with it. It's very unattractive and it comes across poorly. You can still survive with it if you explain what you're doing. And it really helps if you at least know what AFR is, what imputed interest income is, and the general risk that you're asking the seller to take. If that's news to you for the first time, don't put it in your LOI. Make a better offer or at least have your seller financing be at the applicable federal rate so that you take that off the table altogether. If you found this valuable at all, please like and subscribe or check out dealacademy.org
description:
Let’s be real—most Letters of Intent (LOIs) look straight-up stupid. In this video, we break down the common mistakes buyers make when drafting an LOI, from offering zero money down to vague terms that turn sellers off instantly. If you’re serious about buying a business, your LOI needs to reflect it. We’ll walk through the red flags, the rookie moves, and how to craft an LOI that actually gets taken seriously—and gets the deal done.
